questions.q: A 28-year-old man with borderline tuberculoid leprosy presents with sudden onset of painful, erythematous, oedematous skin lesions over his existing patches and acute facial nerve palsy. He completed MDT one month ago. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.exp: This is a Type 1 (reversal) reaction in leprosy, characterised by upgrading immune response with oedematous skin lesions and acute neuritis/nerve palsy. Treatment of choice is systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 40–60 mg/day tapered over months) to prevent permanent nerve damage. Thalidomide is used for Type 2 (ENL) reactions, not Type 1.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters involving the oral mucosa and skin. Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis and 'tombstone' pattern of basal cells. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposits in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. Which antibody is primarily responsible?
questions.exp: This is pemphigus vulgaris with mucosal involvement. Anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies target desmoglein 3 (predominantly expressed in mucosae), causing mucocutaneous disease. Anti-desmoglein 1 causes pemphigus foliaceus (superficial, no mucosal involvement). Anti-BP180 is seen in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 32-year-old sex worker presents with a painless indurated genital ulcer present for 2 weeks. Dark-field microscopy shows motile spirochaetes. VDRL titre is 1:128. Which stage of syphilis and recommended treatment (assuming no penicillin allergy)?
opts: Secondary syphilis; Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
Primary syphilis; Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
Primary syphilis; Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 28 days
Latent syphilis; Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM weekly × 3
questions.exp: A painless indurated ulcer (chancre) with positive dark-field microscopy indicates primary syphilis. The high VDRL titre confirms active infection. Treatment of primary syphilis is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose. Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days is the alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 10-year-old boy from a rural area presents with broken hairs ('black dot' pattern) and occipital lymphadenopathy. KOH mount shows endothrix hair invasion. Which organism and best treatment?
opts: Trichophyton violaceum; Griseofulvin 20 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks
Microsporum canis; Terbinafine 250 mg/day for 4 weeks
Trichophyton tonsurans; Itraconazole 100 mg/day for 8 weeks
Microsporum audouinii; Fluconazole 6 mg/kg/week for 4 weeks
questions.exp: Endothrix tinea capitis (black dot pattern) in India is most commonly caused by Trichophyton violaceum. Griseofulvin (20 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks) remains the drug of choice for tinea capitis in children as it concentrates in keratinised tissue. Terbinafine is less effective against Trichophyton violaceum than griseofulvin in endemic regions.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman with known SLE presents with a photosensitive facial rash, discoid lesions, oral ulcers, and alopecia. Which antibody is most specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity (especially nephritis)?
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA antibody is highly specific for SLE (~95% specificity) and its titre correlates with disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis. Anti-Sm is very specific (~99%) but does not correlate with activity. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with neonatal lupus and subacute cutaneous lupus. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: An 80-year-old man presents with tense blisters on an erythematous, urticarial base involving the flexures. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. What is the antigen targeted?
questions.exp: This is bullous pemphigoid. The primary pathogenic antigen is BP180 (collagen XVII / BPAG2, 180 kDa), located in hemidesmosomes. Anti-BP180 antibodies (targeting the NC16A domain) are highly sensitive and specific for bullous pemphigoid and correlate with disease activity. BP230 is also targeted but is less clinically significant.

questions.q: A 60-year-old chronic smoker presents with a pearly, nodular lesion on the nose with rolled telangiectatic edges and central crusting. Histology shows palisaded tumour cells with peripheral clefting artefact. What is the most common site and characteristic microscopic feature of this tumour?
opts: Sun-exposed areas, especially nose; peripheral palisading with cleft artefact
questions.exp: This is basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common skin cancer. It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas, especially the nose (most common site). Microscopic features include peripheral nuclear palisading of tumour cells and a retraction cleft (artefact) between tumour islands and stroma. Keratin pearls indicate squamous differentiation (SCC). Pagetoid spread is seen in melanoma in situ and extramammary Paget's disease.

questions.q: A 70-year-old immunocompromised woman develops painful grouped vesicles along the right V1 dermatome involving the tip and side of the nose. Which structure is at highest risk and what is this clinical sign called?
questions.exp: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus involving the nasociliary branch of V1 causes vesicles on the tip and side of the nose — Hutchinson's sign. This predicts ocular involvement (keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma) because the nasociliary nerve supplies both the nasal tip and the globe. Urgent ophthalmology referral and antiviral therapy are mandatory.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops fatigue, pallor, and methaemoglobinaemia. Which enzyme deficiency makes patients most susceptible to dapsone haemolysis?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent haematological toxicity including haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia. G6PD deficiency dramatically increases the risk of severe haemolysis with dapsone because G6PD is essential for the hexose monophosphate shunt that regenerates NADPH, protecting RBCs from oxidative damage. G6PD screening is recommended before starting dapsone.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with an oval, salmon-coloured 'herald patch' on the trunk followed by Christmas tree-like distribution of similar smaller lesions. What is the characteristic orientation of the lesions and expected course?
opts: Perpendicular to skin lines; resolves in 1–2 weeks
Along Langer's lines (skin cleavage lines); self-limiting in 6–8 weeks
Along dermatomes; associated with nerve root involvement
questions.exp: Pityriasis rosea is characterized by a herald patch followed by secondary lesions arranged along Langer's lines in a Christmas tree pattern on the trunk. It is self-limiting, typically resolving in 6–8 weeks without treatment. HHV-6 and HHV-7 have been implicated. Acyclovir may shorten duration if given early, but is not routinely used.

questions.q: A 15-year-old presents with target lesions (concentric rings) involving the acral skin and mucosae after a herpes simplex virus infection 10 days prior. Which pathogenic mechanism best explains erythema multiforme (EM)?
opts: HSV-specific CD8+ T cell-mediated immune response depositing HSV DNA in keratinocytes
Immune complex deposition causing Type III hypersensitivity
questions.exp: EM is primarily triggered by HSV infection. HSV-specific CD8+ T cells recognise HSV DNA (especially pol gene fragment) deposited in keratinocytes, leading to cell-mediated cytotoxicity. This is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction, not IgE-mediated. Differentiating EM from Stevens-Johnson syndrome is important: EM has target lesions, is acral > mucosal, and is mostly HSV-triggered.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with heliotrope discolouration of upper eyelids, V-sign erythema on the anterior chest, Gottron's papules on the knuckles, and proximal muscle weakness. Serum CK is elevated. Which antibody is specifically associated with interstitial lung disease in this condition?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis with anti-Jo-1 antibody (anti-synthetase antibody against histidyl-tRNA synthetase) is strongly associated with interstitial lung disease (ILD), mechanic's hands, arthritis, and Raynaud's phenomenon — the antisynthetase syndrome. Anti-Mi-2 is associated with classic DM with good prognosis. Anti-TIF1-γ is associated with malignancy-associated DM. Anti-MDA5 is associated with clinically amyopathic DM and severe ILD.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with multiple, painful, soft genital ulcers with undermined, ragged edges and unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy with a fluctuant bubo. Gram stain shows 'school of fish' pattern. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. It presents with painful, soft ulcers with undermined ragged edges (unlike the hard, painless chancre of syphilis) and unilateral tender lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain shows gram-negative coccobacilli in a 'school of fish' (railroad track) pattern. Treatment: Azithromycin 1g single dose or Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose.

questions.q: A 10-year-old with junctional epidermolysis bullosa (Herlitz type) presents with blisters at birth. Electron microscopy shows absence of hemidesmosomes. Which protein is most commonly defective?
questions.exp: Junctional EB (Herlitz type) results from mutations in genes encoding laminin 332 (formerly laminin 5; subunits LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2). Laminin 332 is crucial for hemidesmosome function and anchoring the epidermis to the dermis. Keratin 5/14 mutations cause EB simplex (epidermolytic). Type VII collagen mutations cause dystrophic EB. Plectin mutations cause EB with muscular dystrophy.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman on isotretinoin for severe nodulo-cystic acne wants to conceive. She asks when it is safe to stop contraception. What is the recommended waiting period after stopping isotretinoin?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin (a systemic retinoid) is a potent teratogen (Category X). The half-life of isotretinoin is approximately 10–20 hours, with the active metabolite 4-oxo-isotretinoin having a longer half-life (~29 hours). Contraception should be used during treatment and for 1 month after stopping isotretinoin. The drug is fully eliminated within 1 month, so pregnancy can be attempted 1 month after the last dose.

questions.q: A 40-year-old presents with painless inguinal lymphadenopathy with 'groove sign' (inguinal ligament dividing lymph node mass). He had a painless genital papule 3 weeks ago that healed spontaneously. What is the causative organism and serotype?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes L1, L2, L2b, and L3. The groove sign (pathognomonic) results from inguinal and femoral lymph node enlargement separated by the inguinal ligament. Serotypes D–K cause uncomplicated chlamydial urethritis/cervicitis. Treatment: Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with intensely itchy linear burrows between the fingers and on the wrists, worse at night. Other family members are also affected. What is the treatment of choice for a child aged 2–12 years?
questions.exp: 5% Permethrin cream is the first-line treatment for scabies in children aged 2 months and older. It is applied from neck to toe (scalp and face in infants), left overnight (8–12 hours), and rinsed off. Oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg) is an alternative but is not recommended in children under 15 kg. Lindane is avoided due to neurotoxicity risk. All household contacts should be treated simultaneously.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man develops high fever, mucocutaneous involvement >30% BSA, widespread epidermal detachment, and positive Nikolsky sign after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Histology shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis. What is this condition?
questions.exp: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is defined by epidermal detachment >30% BSA. Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) involves <10%, and SJS-TEN overlap 10–30%. TEN shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis on histology, distinguishing it from SSSS (which shows subcorneal cleavage due to exfoliative toxin). Sulfonamides are among the most common drugs causing TEN. SCORTEN score guides prognosis and ICU management.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with depigmented patches on the face, hands, and genitalia. Under Wood's lamp (365 nm), the lesions show bright white fluorescence with accentuation. What is the Wood's lamp finding and the defect in vitiligo?
opts: Bright chalk-white fluorescence; loss of melanocytes
questions.exp: Vitiligo lesions show bright chalk-white or blue-white fluorescence under Wood's lamp (365 nm) due to complete loss of melanocytes (autoimmune destruction). This accentuates the contrast with surrounding normal skin. Coral-red fluorescence is seen in erythrasma (Corynebacterium). Greenish fluorescence is seen in Microsporum tinea capitis. Wood's lamp is particularly useful to detect lesions in fair-skinned individuals and to differentiate vitiligo from other hypopigmentation disorders.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presents with calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias. Which antibody is associated with this pattern?
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis) is associated with anti-centromere antibody (ACA) in 70–80% of patients. ACA is associated with a more benign course, later onset of pulmonary arterial hypertension, and relatively spared renal involvement. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and worse prognosis (ILD). Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with diffuse SSc and scleroderma renal crisis.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the most likely organism and first-line topical treatment?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is the most common bacterial skin infection in children, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters). First-line topical treatment is mupirocin 2% ointment TID for 5 days or fusidic acid cream. Mupirocin is preferred where S. aureus is the predominant pathogen. Systemic antibiotics (cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate) are used for extensive or recurrent impetigo.

questions.q: A 50-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 count of 100 cells/μL develops violaceous, non-tender nodules and plaques on the lower extremities, oral mucosa, and visceral organs. Skin biopsy shows spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated RBCs. Which virus is associated?
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8 / Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus, KSHV). It is the most common AIDS-defining malignancy. Classic KS is seen in elderly Mediterranean men; epidemic KS occurs in HIV-positive patients with low CD4 counts. Histology shows proliferating spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, and haemosiderin deposits. ART initiation is the cornerstone of management for epidemic KS.

questions.q: A patient with suspected nickel allergy from jewellery undergoes patch testing. The patch test is applied to the upper back and read at 48 hours showing erythema and vesicles, and again at 96 hours showing persistent reaction. What does a 'crescendo reaction' (worsening from 48h to 96h) indicate?
questions.exp: In patch testing, a crescendo reaction (worsening or maintained intensity from 48h to 96h reading) indicates true allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV delayed hypersensitivity). An irritant reaction typically peaks at 48h and fades by 96h (decrescendo pattern). Readings at D2 (48h) and D4 (96h) or D7 are essential. The ICDRG grading uses +, ++, +++ for erythema, papules, vesicles, and bullae respectively.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman on phenolphthalein (previously) now on NSAIDs develops a recurring oval hyperpigmented patch at the same site on the lip and hand every time she takes the drug. What is the pathogenic mechanism?
opts: Type I IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
Intraepidermal CD8+ effector memory T cells causing localised cytotoxicity
Immune complex deposition at dermal vessels
Molecular mimicry between drug and epidermal antigen
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption (FDE) recurs at the same site with re-exposure to the offending drug. It is mediated by intraepidermal CD8+ effector memory T cells (Tem) that persist in the lesional skin long after the acute episode. Upon drug re-exposure, these Tem cells are activated, releasing IFN-γ and cytotoxic mediators, causing the characteristic localised bullous or erosive lesion followed by post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp. Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae. With which gastrointestinal condition is this associated?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is strongly associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). Granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips on DIF are pathognomonic. Anti-epidermal transglutaminase (eTG, TG3) antibodies are the primary autoantigen; anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies are used for diagnosis. Strict gluten-free diet is the treatment of choice; dapsone provides rapid relief of itch.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man has well-demarcated silvery-scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces with pitting of all fingernails, onycholysis, and 'oil drop' sign. Which nail change is most specific for psoriasis?
questions.exp: The salmon patch or oil drop sign (a yellow-brown discolouration under the nail plate) is most specific for psoriasis, caused by psoriatic involvement of the nail bed. Pitting is the most common nail change in psoriasis (from matrix involvement) but can also occur in alopecia areata. Onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis are common but not specific to psoriasis. Beau's lines and leukonychia are non-specific.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man presents with widespread erythroderma (>90% BSA), peripheral eosinophilia, and a skin biopsy showing epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes with Pautrier microabscesses and 'haloed' lymphocytes. CD4:CD8 ratio is 10:1. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF) in its late stage can present as erythroderma. Pautrier microabscesses (intraepidermal clusters of atypical CD4+ T cells) and epidermotropism are hallmarks of MF histology. Sézary syndrome is the leukemic variant of MF with erythroderma + circulating Sézary cells (≥1000 cells/μL). The distinction is critical: Sézary syndrome requires peripheral blood involvement. ATLL is associated with HTLV-1.

questions.q: During dermoscopy of a 4 mm pigmented lesion on the back of a 45-year-old patient, you observe an atypical pigment network, irregular dots/globules, regression structures (white scar-like areas + blue-grey peppering), and a blue-white veil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Melanoma-specific dermoscopic features include: atypical pigment network, irregular streaks (radial streaming/pseudopods), regression structures (white scar-like areas + blue-grey peppering/granularity), blue-white veil (overlying diffuse irregular pigmentation), and atypical vascular patterns. The combination of multiple specific features strongly suggests melanoma. Pigmented BCC shows blue-grey ovoid nests, leaf-like areas, and spoke-wheel structures.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with diffuse non-scarring alopecia, exclamation mark hairs, and a single 5 cm bald patch on the scalp. Trichoscopy reveals yellow dots and short vellus hairs. Nail examination shows regular fine pits (geometric/grid-like pattern). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Alopecia areata (AA) is characterised by non-scarring alopecia with exclamation mark hairs (broken hairs tapered at the base), yellow dots (empty follicular ostia with sebum) on dermoscopy/trichoscopy, and geometric nail pitting. The geometric or grid-like pitting pattern is more specific for AA than psoriasis (which shows irregular pitting). AA is an autoimmune T-cell-mediated condition targeting anagen follicles.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man who returned from a forest area presents with a verrucous nodule on his right index finger with ascending lymphangitis (sporotrichoid spread). KOH mount is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?
opts: Sporotrichosis; saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI) or itraconazole
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis (caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a thermally dimorphic fungus) classically presents with a primary inoculation lesion followed by nodular lymphangitis with sporotrichoid spread along lymphatics. It is associated with plant/soil exposure (rose thorns, moss). Treatment: SSKI 5 drops TID escalating to 40–50 drops TID (cheap and effective for lymphocutaneous form) or itraconazole 100–200 mg/day for 3–6 months.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with borderline lepromatous leprosy develops sudden onset fever, multiple tender erythematous nodules over the body, joint pain, orchitis, and peripheral neuritis. Serum shows elevated ESR and C-reactive protein. What is this reaction and the drug of choice?
opts: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction; continue MDT without change
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) occurs in lepromatous (LL) and borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III) reaction with systemic features (fever, arthralgia, orchitis, iridocyclitis, neuritis). Thalidomide (100–400 mg/day) is the drug of choice for ENL, especially recurrent/chronic ENL in males. Prednisolone is an alternative. Clofazimine 300 mg/day has anti-inflammatory properties and is used for chronic ENL.
